As in the Muse Spark Safety & Preparedness Report, we consider two related threat scenarios—monitor evasion (the model evades monitors through behavioral adaptation) and monitor interference (the model disables or corrupts monitoring systems)—and evaluate whether Muse Spark 1.1 substantially contributes to either, independent of the current state of Meta’s deployment monitoring. Threat model. Both scenarios share a foundational prerequisite: covert-action capability—the ability to accomplish an objective while evading monitoring. As in the Muse Spark Safety & Preparedness Report, we conservatively assume misaligned objectives for threat-modeling purposes and focus on the observable capabilities and propensities that would enable these threats; see the Muse Spark Safety & Preparedness Report for the full sequential conditions for each scenario. Methodology. Following the Muse Spark Safety & Preparedness Report, we use a two-stage approach. The capability assessment measures whether Muse Spark 1.1 can accomplish side objectives while evading monitoring, and can reason about and act on implicit environmental constraints, using SHADE-Arena (Kutasov et al., 2025), GDM-Stealth, and GDM Situational Awareness (Phuong et al., 2025); benchmark construction, monitors, and indicative thresholds are as described in the Muse Spark Safety & Preparedness Report. Assessment. In the Muse Spark Safety & Preparedness Report, Muse Spark 1.0 did not substantially contribute to either scenario: covert-action capability was limited (side-task success under active monitoring fell well below the indicative thresholds), and situational awareness was constrained. This is confirmed for Muse Spark 1.1. Results. On SHADE-Arena, Muse Spark 1.1 shows increased capabilities in performing both the main and side tasks successfully, indeed beating the comparison models. However, chain-of-thought monitors lower the overall success rate to 6.8% Figure 23. Table 9 shows that Muse Spark 1.1 still underperforms humans in GDM-Stealth tasks, resolving 2 out of 4, while on GDM Situational Awareness (Table 10) Muse Spark 1.1 resolves 7 out of 11 tasks, which is on-par with comparison models, and still below the indicative threshold that would prompt further investigation. 44 Model Challenges Pass (%) Avg Success Rate Muse Spark 1.1 7/11 63.6 55.1 Muse Spark 1.1 Helpful 5/11 45.6 45.8 GPT-5.5 7/11 63.6 60.0 Gemini 3.1 Pro 7/11 63.6 54.5 Claude Opus 4.8 7/11 63.6 53.1 Table 10 GDM Situational Awareness aggregated results. For Muse Spark 1.1 and comparison models, the table reports the number of solved challenges (success score above 20%), its relative number, and the model average success score rate. Higher scores demonstrate higher situational awareness. 2.3.3 Misaligned Propensities In addition to the targeted evaluations for each threat scenario, we consider standalone propensity evaluations—run as part of the model behavior assessment for Muse Spark 1.1 (Section 4)—as an additional signal of whether the model’s general behavioral profile is consistent with safe deployment. As in the Muse Spark Safety & Preparedness Report, we treat the following as having cross-cutting implications for our loss of control threat models: • MASK (Ren et al., 2025): tests how robustly the model maintains epistemic integrity (honesty) when pressured to contradict its baseline knowledge, with implications for the robustness of oversight mechanisms. • Agentic Misalignment (Lynch et al., 2025): tests how readily the model, instantiated as an agent, engages in harmful actions that serve its objective or protect it from being replaced or shut down. With the Muse Spark 1.1 API exposing agentic affordances, this scenario is directly relevant to the deployed configuration. Assessment. As reported in our model behavior assessment for Muse Spark 1.1, the model robustly maintains its epistemic integrity, achieving 95.7% honesty score on MASK, and it shows a low tendency toward self-preservation under pressure, getting a 1.1% harmful action rate across all tasks on Agentic Misalignment (Section 1.1.3). We detected high rates of verbalized evaluation awareness for Agentic Misalignment ( 79%), along with statistical significant performance differences between rollouts where awareness is verbalized and those where it is not.
